lessons.title: What bio-security is and why it matters
lessons.html:
What bio-security is and why it matters

Bio-security means all the things we do to keep diseases out of the farm and to stop them spreading from one house to another. Germs are too small to see. They travel on people, boots, clothes, vehicles, crates, wild birds, rats and flies.

Why it matters

Some poultry diseases, like bird flu (avian influenza) and Newcastle disease, can kill many birds very fast. When bird flu has broken out in South Africa, millions of birds have had to be killed. A farm can lose its whole flock and its income. Some diseases must by law be reported to the state vet under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

How germs get in

  • People: on hands, boots and clothes, especially people who keep their own chickens at home.
  • Vehicles: feed trucks, bakkies and egg trucks bring dirt on their wheels.
  • Equipment: crates, trays and tools moved between farms or houses.
  • Wild birds, rats and mice: they carry germs and eat feed.
  • Dead birds: left lying around, they attract dogs, jackals and flies.
  • Dirty water and feed.

Your part

Bio-security only works if every worker follows the rules every day. One person who skips the foot bath can bring disease into a house of thousands of birds. Do not keep your own chickens or pigeons at home if the farm rules say so, and never bring birds onto the farm.

Visitors

Visitors are a big risk. Only people with a reason to be there may enter. They must sign the book, wear clean farm clothes and boots, and should not have been on another poultry farm recently. Ask your supervisor before you let anyone in.

lessons.title: Bio-security rules in daily work
lessons.html:
Bio-security rules in daily work

Entering the farm and the house

  1. Sign the visitors or entry book at the gate.
  2. Vehicles drive through the wheel bath or are sprayed at the gate.
  3. Shower in and change into farm clothes and boots if your farm has a shower block.
  4. Step into the foot bath at every house door. Brush off mud first, because dirt stops the disinfectant working.
  5. Wash or sanitise your hands.

Foot baths

  • Keep them filled with the correct disinfectant mixed as the label says.
  • Change them when they are dirty or as often as the farm rule says.
  • Wear gloves and eye protection when you mix disinfectant.

Working order

Work from the youngest birds to the oldest, and from healthy houses to sick houses. Never go from a sick house back to young chicks on the same day without a full change and wash.

Dead birds

  • Collect dead birds every day.
  • Put them in the closed bin or take them to the incinerator, pit or composting place the farm uses.
  • Never throw them in the veld or give them to dogs.

Pests and wild birds

  • Keep doors and nets closed so wild birds cannot get in.
  • Clean up spilt feed.
  • Report rats and holes in walls.
  • Only trained staff may handle rat poison.

Report at once

Tell your supervisor straight away if many birds die suddenly, birds have swollen heads, stop eating or drinking, or eggs drop sharply.

Key points

  • Bio-security keeps disease out and stops it spreading.
  • Germs travel on people, vehicles, equipment, pests and wild birds.
  • Use the foot bath at every door and brush off mud first.
  • Work from young to old and from healthy to sick.
  • Remove dead birds daily and report sudden deaths at once.
